edition.copy_text: Koetschau, GCS 2–3 (1899), via the Perseus TEI

source_text: Ἐπεὶ δέ φησιν ὅτι πάντων ἀκούσει τῶν ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον διεστηκότων λεγόντων τό· „ἐμοὶ κόσμος ἐσταύρωται, κἀγὼ κόσμῳ,“ καὶ τοῦτο ψεῦδος διελέγξομεν. εἰσὶ γάρ τινες αἱρέσεις τὰς Παύλου ἐπιστολὰς τοῦ ἀποστόλου μὴ προσιέμεναι, ὥσπερ Ἐβιωναῖοι ἀμφότεροι καὶ οἱ καλούμενοι Ἐγκρατηταί. οὐκ ἂν οὖν οἱ μὴ χρώμενοι τῷ ἀποστόλῳ ὡς μακαρίῳ τινὶ καὶ σοφῷ λέγοιεν τό· „ἐμοὶ κόσμος ἐσταύρωται, κἀγὼ κόσμῳ“· διὸ καὶ ἐν τούτῳ ὁ Κέλσος ψεύδεται. καὶ ἐπιδιατρίβει γε κατηγορῶν τῆς ἐν ταῖς αἱρέσεσι διαφορᾶς· οὐ πάνυ δέ μοι δοκεῖ διαρθροῦν ἃ λέγει οὐδ᾿ ἐπιμελῶς αὐτὰ τεθεωρηκέναι οὐδὲ κατανενοηκέναι, πῶς πλεῖον Ἰουδαίων ἐπίστασθαι λέγουσιν ἑαυτοὺς οἱ ἐν τοῖς λόγοις διαβεβηκότες Χριστιανοὶ, καὶ πότερον τοῖς μὲν βιβλίοις συγκατατιθέμενοι τὸν δὲ νοῦν ἀντεξηγούμενοι, ἢ οὐδὲ συγκατατιθέμενοι τοῖς ἐκείνων γράμμασιν· ἑκάτερα γὰρ εὕροιμεν ἂν ἐν ταῖς αἱρέσεσι. μετὰ ταῦτά φησι· φέρ᾿ οὖν, εἰ καὶ μηδεμίαν ἀρχὴν τοῦ δόγματος ἔχουσιν, αὐτὸν ἐξετάσωμεν τὸν λόγον· πρότερον δὲ ὅσα παρακηκοότες ὑπ᾿ ἀγνοίας διαφθείρουσιν, οὐκ ἐμμελῶς ἐν ἀρχαῖς εὐθὺς ἀπαυθαδιαζόμενοι περὶ ὧν οὐκ ἴσασι, λεκτέον· ἔστι δὲ τάδε. καὶ εὐθέως λέξεσί τισι, τοῖς πιστεύουσι τῷ Χριστιανῶν λόγῳ συνεχῶς ὀνομαζομέναις, ἀντιπαρατίθησιν ἀπὸ τῶν φιλοσόφων, βουλόμενος τὰ καλὰ τῶν νομιζομένων Κέλσῳ παρὰ Χριστιανοῖς λέγεσθαι καὶ βέλτιον καὶ τρανότερον εἰρῆσθαι παρὰ τοῖς φιλοσοφοῦσιν, ἵνα περισπάσῃ ἐπὶ φιλοσοφίαν τοὺς ἁλισκομένους ὑπὸ τῶν αὐτόθεν ἐμφαινόντων δογμάτων τὸ καλὸν καὶ τὸ εὐσεβές. καὶ τὸν πέμπτον δὴ τόμον αὐτόθι καταπαύσαντες ἀρξώμεθα τοῦ ἕκτου ἀπὸ τῶν ἑξῆς.
pass_a_gloss: Since he says that he/one will hear (ἀκούω, fut.) all those standing apart (διίστημι) to such a degree saying: 'The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world,' we shall refute (διελέγχω) this too as a falsehood (ψεῦδος). For there are some sects (αἱρέσεις) not accepting (προσίεμαι) the letters (ἐπιστολαί) of Paul the apostle, as both (ἀμφότεροι) Ebionites (Ἐβιωναῖοι) and the so-called Encratites (Ἐγκρατηταί). Those then not using (χράομαι) the apostle as someone blessed (μακάριος) and wise (σοφός) would not say: 'The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world'; therefore in this too Celsus lies (ψεύδομαι). And he lingers (ἐπιδιατρίβω) accusing (κατηγορέω) the difference (διαφορά) in the sects; but he does not at all seem to me to articulate (διαρθρόω) what he says nor carefully (ἐπιμελῶς) to have contemplated (θεωρέω) them nor understood (κατανοέω) how the Christians who have stood firm/taken their stand (διαβαίνω, perf. part.) in the doctrines (λόγοι) say they know (ἐπίσταμαι) more than Jews, and whether assenting (συγκατατίθεμαι) to the books but interpreting the sense (νοῦς) otherwise (ἀντεξηγέομαι), or not even assenting to their writings (γράμματα); for we would find both in the sects. After this he says: 'Come then, even if they have no starting point/basis (ἀρχή) of the doctrine (δόγμα), let us examine (ἐξετάζω) the teaching (λόγος) itself; but first must be said the things which, having misheard (παρακούω), they corrupt (διαφθείρω) through ignorance (ἄγνοια), out of tune/unfittingly (οὐκ ἐμμελῶς) at the beginnings straightway behaving arrogantly (ἀπαυθαδιάζομαι) about what they do not know; and they are these.' And at once against certain expressions (λέξεις) continually named by those believing the Christians' teaching he sets in opposition (ἀντιπαρατίθημι) [sayings] from the philosophers, wishing the fine things of those supposed by Celsus to be said among Christians to have been said both better and more clearly (τρανότερον) among those who philosophize, so that he may drag away (περισπάω) to philosophy those caught (ἁλίσκομαι) by doctrines that on their face (αὐτόθεν) display (ἐμφαίνω) the good (τὸ καλόν) and the pious (τὸ εὐσεβές). And having ended (καταπαύω) the fifth volume (τόμος) here, let us begin the sixth from what follows (τὰ ἑξῆς).

pass_b_english: Since he says that “you will hear all those who are so far divided saying, ‘The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world’ ” (Galatians 6:14), we shall show that this too is false. For there are some sects that do not accept the epistles of Paul the apostle, such as the Ebionites of both kinds and those called Encratites. Those, then, who do not treat the apostle as a blessed and wise man would not say: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14). So in this too Celsus lies.

He also spends a long time denouncing the differences among the sects. But he does not seem to me at all to set out clearly what he says, nor to have studied these things carefully, nor to have understood how the Christians who are well grounded in the teachings say that they know more than the Jews, and whether they do so while accepting the books but giving their meaning a rival interpretation, or without even accepting the Jews’ writings. For we would find both among the sects.

After this he says: “Come, then: even if they have no basis for their doctrine, let us examine the teaching itself. But first we must speak of all the things they have misheard and corrupt through ignorance, since right from the start they speak with ill-judged arrogance about things they do not know. These are as follows.” And at once he sets passages from the philosophers against certain expressions that those who believe the Christians’ teaching use constantly. He wants to make out that whatever good things Celsus supposes are said among Christians have been said both better and more clearly by those who practise philosophy, so that he may draw away to philosophy those who are won over by doctrines that show at first sight what is noble and godly.
And so, bringing the fifth book to a close at this point, let us begin the sixth with what comes next.
notes: The 'two kinds of Ebionites' (ἀμφότεροι) are those Origen described in 5.61: one group confessing the virgin birth, the other not. Origen's first sentence restates Celsus's words from 5.64 in indirect form; ἀκούσει is rendered 'you will hear', as there. οἱ ἐν τοῖς λόγοις διαβεβηκότες Χριστιανοί is doubtful: διαβαίνω in the perfect can mean 'stand firm' (rendered 'who are well grounded in the teachings'); it might also be taken as 'who have gone far in the doctrines'. The context concerns the differing sects and Celsus's charge (not preserved verbatim here) that they claim to know more than the Jews. ἀρχή in Celsus's sentence may mean 'basis' or 'starting point'; rendered 'basis'. οὐκ ἐμμελῶς ('out of tune') rendered 'ill-judged'; ἐν ἀρχαῖς εὐθύς rendered 'right from the start'. τοῖς φιλοσοφοῦσιν rendered 'those who practise philosophy' to keep it apart from τῶν φιλοσόφων ('the philosophers'). τόμος ('volume') rendered 'book' for the reader. Galatians 6:14 is cited at each of its two quotations, as the QA gate requires.

Open doubt (review): 5.65 οἱ ἐν τοῖς λόγοις διαβεβηκότες Χριστιανοί is a doubtful reading. It is rendered 'well grounded in the teachings', and the note gives the other sense, 'gone far in the doctrines'. Both chapters still pass, but the owner may want to look at this.
